Reference: Colas and Reynier (2026)

Model Setting

The paper studies the optimal design of spatially differentiated subsidies for residential solar panels in the U.S. The environmental benefit of a rooftop panel depends on where it is installed: how much sunlight it gets, and which power plants its output displaces at each hour. Current subsidies are set state by state and vary widely (the present value for a 15-panel system ranges from under $6,000 in states with only the federal credit to nearly $29,000 in New Jersey), so they may allocate panels to the wrong places. The paper combines a model of household solar demand with a model of hourly power plant dispatch and pollution damages, estimates it with (1) satellite data on rooftop panels (DeepSolar, Google Project Sunroof), (2) hourly plant-level production and emissions (Open Grid Emissions), and (3) the AP3 air pollution model, and solves for the nationally optimal subsidies.

The model has three blocks: (1) households choose whether to install and how many panels, given electricity prices, installation prices, sunlight and three types of state subsidies; (2) residential solar and nondispatchable plants (wind, solar) produce first, and dispatchable plants respond to the remaining excess load through plant-specific policy functions with capacity and nonnegativity constraints; (3) dispatchable production maps into emissions and damages. A government chooses subsidies in every state to maximize household utility minus environmental damages subject to a budget constraint. The analysis is partial equilibrium and long run: installation prices and electricity prices are fixed, there are no peer effects, and subsidies are constant over time.

Electricity Production

Three sources supply electricity: residential solar, nondispatchable plants and dispatchable plants. Let RRR index NERC regions (seven, with California separated from WECC). Residential solar production in region RRR in hour ttt is ERtSolar=∫i∈IRmi⋆Ni⋆AitdiE_{Rt}^{Solar}=\int_{i\in I_R}m_i^\star N_i^\star A_{it}diERtSolar​=∫i∈IR​​mi⋆​Ni⋆​Ait​di, and nondispatchable production is ERtNonD=∑k∈KRyktNonDE_{Rt}^{NonD}=\sum_{k\in K_R}y_{kt}^{NonD}ERtNonD​=∑k∈KR​​yktNonD​, which depends only on environmental conditions (sun, wind) and is curtailed only if it would exceed demand. The excess load that must be met by dispatchable plants is:

ELoadRt=LoadRt−ERtNonD−ERtSolar(8.5.2.9)ELoad_{Rt}=Load_{Rt}-E_{Rt}^{NonD}-E_{Rt}^{Solar} \tag{8.5.2.9}ELoadRt​=LoadRt​−ERtNonD​−ERtSolar​(8.5.2.9)

Balancing authorities dispatch plants centrally, so production by dispatchable plant kkk is modeled as a reduced-form policy function of excess loads, with nonnegativity and capacity constraints:

yktDisp={0if fk(ELoadt,εkt)≤0,fk(ELoadt,εkt)if 0<fk(ELoadt,εkt)<yˉk,yˉkif fk(ELoadt,εkt)≥yˉk,(8.5.2.10)y_{kt}^{Disp}=\begin{cases}0 & \text{if } f_k(ELoad_t,\varepsilon_{kt})\le 0,\\ f_k(ELoad_t,\varepsilon_{kt}) & \text{if } 0<f_k(ELoad_t,\varepsilon_{kt})<\bar{y}_k,\\ \bar{y}_k & \text{if } f_k(ELoad_t,\varepsilon_{kt})\ge\bar{y}_k,\end{cases} \tag{8.5.2.10}yktDisp​=⎩⎨⎧​0fk​(ELoadt​,εkt​)yˉ​k​​if fk​(ELoadt​,εkt​)≤0,if 0<fk​(ELoadt​,εkt​)<yˉ​k​,if fk​(ELoadt​,εkt​)≥yˉ​k​,​(8.5.2.10)

where yˉk\bar{y}_kyˉ​k​ is nameplate capacity, ELoadtELoad_tELoadt​ is the vector of excess loads across regions, and fkf_kfk​ is a plant-specific latent function, a quadratic in the excess load of every region R∈RkR\in\mathbf{R}_kR∈Rk​ in plant kkk's interconnection (East, West, Texas):

fk(ELoadt,εkt)=ψk0+∑R∈Rk(ψRk1ELoadRt+ψRk2ELoadRt2)+εkt,εkt∼N(0,σk2)(8.5.2.11)f_k(ELoad_t,\varepsilon_{kt})=\psi_k^0+\sum_{R\in\mathbf{R}_k}\left(\psi_{Rk}^1ELoad_{Rt}+\psi_{Rk}^2ELoad_{Rt}^2\right)+\varepsilon_{kt},\qquad \varepsilon_{kt}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_k^2) \tag{8.5.2.11}fk​(ELoadt​,εkt​)=ψk0​+R∈Rk​∑​(ψRk1​ELoadRt​+ψRk2​ELoadRt2​)+εkt​,εkt​∼N(0,σk2​)(8.5.2.11)

So yktDispy_{kt}^{Disp}yktDisp​ is a plant-specific Tobit, censored at 0 and yˉk\bar{y}_kyˉ​k​. ψk0\psi_k^0ψk0​ captures the plant's position in the dispatch order (a very negative value means the plant only runs at very high excess load, i.e. a peaker), ψRk1,ψRk2\psi_{Rk}^1,\psi_{Rk}^2ψRk1​,ψRk2​ capture how intensively it is dispatched and how much its output responds to load in other regions (transmission across regions within an interconnection). fkf_kfk​ is constrained to be weakly increasing in excess load.

Unlike marginal-emissions regressions in which hour-specific coefficients are fixed (Holland et al. 2016; Sexton et al. 2021), here production, and hence marginal emissions, respond endogenously to large changes in residential solar. Identification uses variation in both demand and nondispatchable output.

Damages

Let g∈G={NOx,PM2.5,SO2,CO2e}g\in\mathcal{G}=\{NO_x,PM_{2.5},SO_2,CO_2e\}g∈G={NOx​,PM2.5​,SO2​,CO2​e}. Marginal emission rates decline with utilization, so emissions are a plant-specific linear spline in production with a kink at the plant's median positive production yk50y_k^{50}yk50​:

Total damages in hour ttt are Dt(ELoadt)=∑kdkt(yktDisp)D_t(ELoad_t)=\sum_kd_{kt}(y_{kt}^{Disp})Dt​(ELoadt​)=∑k​dkt​(yktDisp​), and the present value is D(ELoad)=∑t=0T[Dt(ELoadt)/(1+r)t]D(ELoad)=\sum_{t=0}^T[D_t(ELoad_t)/(1+r)^t]D(ELoad)=∑t=0T​[Dt​(ELoadt​)/(1+r)t]. The external benefit of one more panel installed by household iii is the damage it offsets over its lifetime:

It varies across space (sunlight AitA_{it}Ait​, regional plant mix) and over hours (which plants are marginal at that excess load).

where λ\lambdaλ is the marginal cost of public funds.   • Extensive margin: the number of additional households induced to install, ∂Mj/∂sjθ=∫i∈Ijmi→θdi\partial M_j/\partial s_j^\theta=\int_{i\in I_j}\overrightarrow{m_i}^{\theta}di∂Mj​/∂sjθ​=∫i∈Ij​​mi​​θdi, times the gap between their average damages offset ΔDj→θ,ext\overrightarrow{\Delta D_j}^{\theta,ext}ΔDj​​θ,ext (evaluated at the excess load under the optimal subsidies) and the shadow cost of their average subsidy λsj→θ,ext\lambda\overrightarrow{s_j}^{\theta,ext}λsj​​θ,ext.

The government raises subsidies where they induce many additional panels with large environmental benefits at low fiscal cost. Because marginal damages, the number of marginal households and the number of nonadditional households all change with the subsidy system, the optimum has to be solved numerically in the estimated model.

Estimation

Data. DeepSolar (2016) gives tract-level numbers of residential systems and panel area (hence panels per system); Google Project Sunroof gives the distribution of suitable rooftop sizes (Nˉi\bar{N}_iNˉi​) and yearly solar potential for 56,940 tracts, combined with NREL SAM hourly profiles by county and 0.5% annual panel degradation to build AitA_{it}Ait​. Subsidies in 2017 come from Sexton et al. (2021) (DSIRE); retail prices from EIA; r=2%r=2\%r=2%; installation price functions from Tracking the Sun by census region. Open Grid Emissions (2019) gives hourly production and emissions for nearly 10,000 plants; 4,625 dispatchable plants with positive, nonconstant output give over 40 million plant-hour observations.

Households (6 parameters: σ,γ0,γColl,γPol,γ1N,γ2N\sigma,\gamma_0,\gamma_{Coll},\gamma_{Pol},\gamma_{1N},\gamma_{2N}σ,γ0​,γColl​,γPol​,γ1N​,γ2N​) are estimated by indirect inference. The main auxiliary model is a border discontinuity regression on tracts within 10 miles of state borders:

log⁡Mℓ=αμℓ+bZℓ+ωborder(ℓ)+εℓ(8.5.2.18)\log M_\ell=\alpha\mu_\ell+bZ_\ell+\omega_{border(\ell)}+\varepsilon_\ell \tag{8.5.2.18}logMℓ​=αμℓ​+bZℓ​+ωborder(ℓ)​+εℓ​(8.5.2.18)

where MℓM_\ellMℓ​ is the number of installations in tract ℓ\ellℓ, μℓ\mu_\ellμℓ​ the average monetary benefit of a 15-panel system, ZℓZ_\ellZℓ​ demographic and state tax controls (income, sales, property taxes), and ωborder(ℓ)\omega_{border(\ell)}ωborder(ℓ)​ a state-pair border fixed effect. Crossing to the more generous side of a border raises the monetary benefit by about $8,000 and installations per capita by about 50%, with no discontinuity in education, partisanship or income. The other auxiliary moments are log installations per household in each tract and the average number of panels per system in each tract.

Dispatchable plants: the Tobit policy functions are estimated plant by plant by maximum likelihood. Damages: the emission splines are estimated by OLS on OGE data, and δgk\delta_{gk}δgk​ is taken from AP3 by matching each plant's county and stack height.

Identification

  • σ\sigmaσ: from the border-discontinuity coefficient α\alphaα, since 1/σ1/\sigma1/σ is the response of installations to monetary benefits. This is causal if preferences for solar are continuous at state borders.

  • γ0,γColl,γPol\gamma_0,\gamma_{Coll},\gamma_{Pol}γ0​,γColl​,γPol​: from how installation rates vary with tract demographics.

  • γ1N,γ2N\gamma_{1N},\gamma_{2N}γ1N​,γ2N​: from the average number of panels per system and how system size varies across places with different monetary benefits.

  • ψk0,ψRk1,ψRk2,σk\psi_k^0,\psi_{Rk}^1,\psi_{Rk}^2,\sigma_kψk0​,ψRk1​,ψRk2​,σk​: from hourly variation in excess load across regions, which comes from both demand and nondispatchable output.

Key Estimates

  • Households (monetary values in $1,000): σ^=11.6\hat{\sigma}=11.6σ^=11.6, so a $1,000 increase in monetary benefits raises installations by about 1/11.6≈9%1/11.6\approx9\%1/11.6≈9%; γ^Coll=7.5\hat{\gamma}_{Coll}=7.5γ^​Coll​=7.5, γ^Pol=17.6\hat{\gamma}_{Pol}=17.6γ^​Pol​=17.6, γ^0=−308.4\hat{\gamma}_0=-308.4γ^​0​=−308.4, γ^1N=34.1\hat{\gamma}_{1N}=34.1γ^​1N​=34.1, γ^2N=−1.1\hat{\gamma}_{2N}=-1.1γ^​2N​=−1.1. Optimal system size barely responds to subsidies: $1,000 more per panel adds only 1/[2(1.1)]≈0.451/[2(1.1)]\approx0.451/[2(1.1)]≈0.45 panels.

  • Validation: implied price elasticity of −0.74-0.74−0.74 (vs. −0.65-0.65−0.65 in Gillingham and Tsvetanov 2019); a $1/W rebate in 12 Northeastern states raises installations by 36% (vs. 47% in Crago and Chernyakhovskiy 2017).

  • Plants: hourly dispatchable output fits with R2R^2R2 of 0.99, 0.96 and 0.96 (East, West, Texas), including afternoon ramping and the fuel mix by excess load.

  • Marginal damages are highest in the East, especially RFC (Mid-Atlantic, lower Great Lakes, coal heavy), and rise with excess load in some regions (NPCC: from $67/MWh to $88/MWh between the 10th and 90th percentiles of excess load), while they are flat in the West and Texas.

Counterfactuals

  • Budget-neutral welfare-maximizing subsidies: optimal subsidies are highest in the Mid-Atlantic and lower Great Lakes and lowest in the Northeast and Northwest (clean grids, little sun). Current installations are about 30% too low in the Midwest and South and 80% too high in the Northeast. Moving to the optimum raises annual damages offset from $262.3M to $292.6M (+11.5%), mostly from CO2_22​e. Almost all adjustment is on the extensive margin.

  • Damage-minimizing subsidies: similar geography with more dispersion (from under $4,000 to over $21,000); damages offset +12.6%.

  • Tract-level subsidies: add little beyond optimal state-level subsidies ($292.9M vs. $292.6M).

  • Unconstrained optimum (no budget constraint): the government maximizes

    ∫iVidi⏟Utility−D(ELoad)⏟Damages−λ∑j∫i∈Ijsijmi⋆di⏟Government cost(8.5.2.19)\underbrace{\int_iV_idi}_{\text{Utility}}-\underbrace{D(ELoad)}_{\text{Damages}}-\lambda\underbrace{\sum_j\int_{i\in I_j}s_{ij}m_i^\star di}_{\text{Government cost}} \tag{8.5.2.19}Utility∫i​Vi​di​​−DamagesD(ELoad)​​−λGovernment costj∑​∫i∈Ij​​sij​mi⋆​di​​(8.5.2.19)

    With λ=1\lambda=1λ=1, annuitized subsidy spending falls from $380.8M to $218.5M and installations to 80% of current levels, achieving 83% of the environmental benefits at 57% of the cost: current national funding exceeds the unconstrained optimum by over 70%. With λ=1.25\lambda=1.25λ=1.25 (1.51.51.5), optimal spending is 23% (under 10%) of current spending.

  • Marginal subsidy increases: damages offset per extra dollar range from $0.22 in Washington to $0.80 in West Virginia (over $0.70 in Ohio and Pennsylvania), so cost-neutral reallocation across states is very valuable.

Extensions

  • Households discounting future subsidies at 15% (as in De Groote and Verboven (2019)): the planner uses mostly upfront cost-based subsidies instead of production subsidies, but the geography and total spending are similar.

  • Line losses (endogenous, following Borenstein and Bushnell 2022): solar is more valuable; cost-neutral gains of 11.4% and 12.3%.

  • Transmission constraints: above the 75th percentile of a region's excess load, plants respond only to their own region's load:

    fk(ELoadt,εkt)={ψk0+∑R′∈Rk(ψR′k1ELoadR′t+ψR′k2ELoadR′t2)+εktif ELoadRt≤ELoad‾R,ψk0,Cons+ψk1,ConsELoadRt+ψk2,ConsELoadRt2+εktif ELoadRt>ELoad‾R.(8.5.2.20)f_k(ELoad_t,\varepsilon_{kt})=\begin{cases}\psi_k^0+\sum_{R'\in\mathbf{R}_k}\left(\psi_{R'k}^1ELoad_{R't}+\psi_{R'k}^2ELoad_{R't}^2\right)+\varepsilon_{kt} & \text{if } ELoad_{Rt}\le\overline{ELoad}_R,\\ \psi_k^{0,Cons}+\psi_k^{1,Cons}ELoad_{Rt}+\psi_k^{2,Cons}ELoad_{Rt}^2+\varepsilon_{kt} & \text{if } ELoad_{Rt}>\overline{ELoad}_R.\end{cases} \tag{8.5.2.20}fk​(ELoadt​,εkt​)={ψk0​+∑R′∈Rk​​(ψR′k1​ELoadR′t​+ψR′k2​ELoadR′t2​)+εkt​ψk0,Cons​+ψk1,Cons​ELoadRt​+ψk2,Cons​ELoadRt2​+εkt​​if ELoadRt​≤ELoadR​,if ELoadRt​>ELoadR​.​(8.5.2.20)

    Current spending then exceeds the optimum by about 45%.

  • Storage and a cleaner grid lower the damages offset by solar and the optimal unconstrained subsidies, but spatial heterogeneity remains, so cost-neutral reallocation still pays off. Optimal subsidies are likely progressive (shifting from rich states such as Massachusetts toward poorer states such as West Virginia).

This is the household's lifetime budget constraint in present value, with uses of funds on the left and sources on the right. All flows over the hours t=0,…,Tt=0,\dots,Tt=0,…,T of the panel's 25-year life are discounted at the real rate rrr, which is why only the discounted sums eie_iei​ and AiA_iAi​ appear.

The first term cic_ici​ is numeraire consumption. The second is the electricity bill: the household consumes eie_iei​ and, if it installs (mi=1m_i=1mi​=1), its NiN_iNi​ panels generate NiAiN_iA_iNi​Ai​, so under net metering it pays the retail price pjp_jpj​ only on the difference. The bill can be negative; every kWh generated is worth exactly pjp_jpj​ regardless of when it is produced, which is what net metering at a constant retail price buys. The third term is the installation price pjIns(Ni)p_j^{Ins}(N_i)pjIns​(Ni​) net of the cost-based subsidy, a share sjCost∈[0,1)s_j^{Cost}\in[0,1)sjCost​∈[0,1). On the right, income yiy_iyi​ is augmented by the production subsidy (sjkWhs_j^{kWh}sjkWh​ per discounted kWh) and the per-panel subsidy (sjPanels_j^{Panel}sjPanel​ per panel).

The three instruments load on different household characteristics:

∂(subsidy receipts)∂sjkWh=NiAi,∂(subsidy receipts)∂sjPanel=Ni,∂(subsidy receipts)∂sjCost=pjIns(Ni).\frac{\partial(\text{subsidy receipts})}{\partial s_j^{kWh}}=N_iA_i,\qquad \frac{\partial(\text{subsidy receipts})}{\partial s_j^{Panel}}=N_i,\qquad \frac{\partial(\text{subsidy receipts})}{\partial s_j^{Cost}}=p_j^{Ins}(N_i).∂sjkWh​∂(subsidy receipts)​=Ni​Ai​,∂sjPanel​∂(subsidy receipts)​=Ni​,∂sjCost​∂(subsidy receipts)​=pjIns​(Ni​).

A production subsidy pays more in sunny places, a cost subsidy pays more where installation is expensive, and a per-panel subsidy pays the same everywhere. The constraint rules out borrowing frictions (everything is a present value) and time-of-use pricing. Solving it for cic_ici​ and substituting into utility (2) gives the installation problem (3) and the monetary benefit (4).

This is the household's objective. It is quasi-linear: numeraire consumption cic_ici​ enters linearly, so utility is measured in (present-value) dollars and there are no income effects on the solar decision. The function νi(⋅)\nu_i(\cdot)νi​(⋅) is the lifetime utility from the whole path of electricity use {eit}\{e_{it}\}{eit​}; it is left unrestricted and household specific. The last term is the nonpecuniary value of owning a system of NiN_iNi​ panels, received only if mi=1m_i=1mi​=1; γi(⋅)\gamma_i(\cdot)γi​(⋅) is strictly concave and collects everything that is not a cash flow: hassle and information costs, aesthetic concerns, environmental preferences, and (in the quantitative model, equation (5)) an idiosyncratic taste draw. It can be, and is estimated to be, very negative on average, which is how the model rationalizes installation rates of about 2 percent despite positive monetary returns in many places.

Two features matter later. First, additive separability between νi\nu_iνi​ and miγi(Ni)m_i\gamma_i(N_i)mi​γi​(Ni​), together with a retail price that does not depend on installation, means the optimal electricity path {eit⋆}\{e_{it}^\star\}{eit⋆​} is the same whether or not the household installs, so there is no rebound effect and the installation problem can be solved separately (equation (3)). Second, linearity in cic_ici​ means a dollar of subsidy raises utility by exactly one dollar, which is what makes the mechanical term in the government's first-order condition (17) equal to 1−λ1-\lambda1−λ per dollar transferred, and lets the government simply add up ViV_iVi​ across households in (14).

This is the parametric form of the nonpecuniary benefit used in the quantitative model. It has three parts.

Excess load is the residual demand that dispatchable plants (coal, gas, nuclear, hydro and so on) must serve in NERC region RRR in hour ttt. It equals total electricity demand LoadRtLoad_{Rt}LoadRt​ minus the two sources that produce first: utility-scale wind and solar, ERtNonDE_{Rt}^{NonD}ERtNonD​, which depend only on weather, and residential rooftop solar, ERtSolarE_{Rt}^{Solar}ERtSolar​, which is the aggregate of household choices. All three are energy quantities (MWh in the hour).

The equation embodies a merit-order assumption: zero-marginal-cost intermittent sources are never displaced by dispatchable ones, so rooftop solar is treated exactly like a reduction in demand. It is the only channel through which households affect the power sector:

∂ELoadRt∂ERtSolar=−1,ERtSolar=∫i∈IRmi⋆Ni⋆Aitdi.\frac{\partial ELoad_{Rt}}{\partial E_{Rt}^{Solar}}=-1,\qquad E_{Rt}^{Solar}=\int_{i\in I_R}m_i^\star N_i^\star A_{it}di .∂ERtSolar​∂ELoadRt​​=−1,ERtSolar​=∫i∈IR​​mi⋆​Ni⋆​Ait​di.

One more kWh from a roof in region RRR lowers that region's excess load by one kWh in the same hour, and through the policy functions (10) and (11) lowers output of whichever plants in the interconnection respond to load in RRR. This is the link used in the derivation of the damages offset (13). Load itself is taken as given (household electricity use does not respond to installation, see equation (3)), and there is no storage in the baseline, so solar offsets generation only in the hours in which the sun shines.

For estimation, excess load is the regressor in the plant-level Tobit, and it varies hour to hour because of both demand and weather-driven nondispatchable output; that variation identifies ψk0,ψRk1,ψRk2\psi_k^0,\psi_{Rk}^1,\psi_{Rk}^2ψk0​,ψRk1​,ψRk2​.

This is the production rule of dispatchable plant kkk: a latent desired output fkf_kfk​ that is censored below at zero (a plant cannot produce negative power) and above at nameplate capacity yˉk\bar{y}_kyˉ​k​. Compactly,

yktDisp=min⁡{yˉk,max⁡{0,fk(ELoadt,εkt)}}.y_{kt}^{Disp}=\min\left\{\bar{y}_k,\max\left\{0,f_k(ELoad_t,\varepsilon_{kt})\right\}\right\}.yktDisp​=min{yˉ​k​,max{0,fk​(ELoadt​,εkt​)}}.

The latent function fkf_kfk​ (equation (11)) is a reduced-form policy function: it summarizes how the balancing authority's dispatch algorithm uses plant kkk as a function of the state of the grid, without modeling bids, marginal costs or transmission explicitly. The argument ELoadtELoad_tELoadt​ is the whole vector of regional excess loads from equation (9), and εkt\varepsilon_{kt}εkt​ is an unobserved shock (outages, fuel prices, ramping constraints).

With the normal shock of equation (11), this is a two-limit Tobit. Writing fˉkt\bar{f}_{kt}fˉ​kt​ for fkf_kfk​ without its shock, the likelihood contribution of one plant-hour is

Lkt={Φ(−fˉkt/σk)if ykt=0,1σkϕ(ykt−fˉktσk)if 0<ykt<yˉk,1−Φ((yˉk−fˉkt)/σk)if ykt=yˉk,L_{kt}=\begin{cases}\Phi\left(-\bar{f}_{kt}/\sigma_k\right) & \text{if } y_{kt}=0,\\ \dfrac{1}{\sigma_k}\phi\left(\dfrac{y_{kt}-\bar{f}_{kt}}{\sigma_k}\right) & \text{if } 0<y_{kt}<\bar{y}_k,\\ 1-\Phi\left(\left(\bar{y}_k-\bar{f}_{kt}\right)/\sigma_k\right) & \text{if } y_{kt}=\bar{y}_k,\end{cases}Lkt​=⎩⎨⎧​Φ(−fˉ​kt​/σk​)σk​1​ϕ(σk​ykt​−fˉ​kt​​)1−Φ((yˉ​k​−fˉ​kt​)/σk​)​if ykt​=0,if 0<ykt​<yˉ​k​,if ykt​=yˉ​k​,​

and each plant's parameters are estimated by maximum likelihood on its own hourly series.

The censoring is what makes marginal emissions endogenous. A baseload plant sits at yˉk\bar{y}_kyˉ​k​ in most hours and does not respond to small load changes; a peaker sits at zero until excess load is high. Which plants are in the interior region, and therefore marginal, changes with the level of excess load, so a large expansion of rooftop solar changes the set of plants it displaces. A regression with fixed hour-specific marginal emission coefficients cannot capture this.

This is the assumed form of the latent dispatch function in equation (10). For plant kkk, desired output is a constant plus a quadratic in the excess load of every NERC region RRR in the set Rk\mathbf{R}_kRk​ of regions in the plant's interconnection (East, West or Texas), plus a normal shock.

The constant ψk0\psi_k^0ψk0​ locates the plant in the dispatch order: a very negative value means fkf_kfk​ becomes positive only at high excess load (a peaker), a large positive value means the plant runs almost always (baseload). The slopes describe how output responds to load in each region,

∂fk∂ELoadRt=ψRk1+2ψRk2ELoadRt ≥0,\frac{\partial f_k}{\partial ELoad_{Rt}}=\psi_{Rk}^1+2\psi_{Rk}^2ELoad_{Rt}\ \ge 0,∂ELoadRt​∂fk​​=ψRk1​+2ψRk2​ELoadRt​ ≥0,

where the inequality is the monotonicity restriction imposed in estimation. Coefficients on regions other than the plant's own capture trade within the interconnection: a plant in one region can ramp up to serve load in a neighboring region. Regions in other interconnections are excluded because the three grids are essentially not connected. The quadratic terms let the response differ between low-load and high-load hours.

Because of the censoring in (10), the response of expected output is the latent slope scaled by the probability of being unconstrained:

∂E[yktDisp]∂ELoadRt=[Φ(yˉk−fˉktσk)−Φ(−fˉktσk)](ψRk1+2ψRk2ELoadRt),\frac{\partial\mathbb{E}\left[y_{kt}^{Disp}\right]}{\partial ELoad_{Rt}}=\left[\Phi\left(\frac{\bar{y}_k-\bar{f}_{kt}}{\sigma_k}\right)-\Phi\left(\frac{-\bar{f}_{kt}}{\sigma_k}\right)\right]\left(\psi_{Rk}^1+2\psi_{Rk}^2ELoad_{Rt}\right),∂ELoadRt​∂E[yktDisp​]​=[Φ(σk​yˉ​k​−fˉ​kt​​)−Φ(σk​−fˉ​kt​​)](ψRk1​+2ψRk2​ELoadRt​),

with fˉkt\bar{f}_{kt}fˉ​kt​ the latent function without its shock. This is the plant-level object behind the marginal damage ∂Dt/∂ERtSolar\partial D_t/\partial E_{Rt}^{Solar}∂Dt​/∂ERtSolar​ in equation (13). The form rules out dynamics (start-up costs, ramping) and interactions between regions; identification comes from hourly variation in excess loads, driven by demand and by wind and solar output. Equation (20) relaxes the specification to allow for transmission congestion.

Two things are left implicit. Production is censored and emissions are kinked, so DtD_tDt​ is differentiable only after taking expectations over the plant shocks εkt\varepsilon_{kt}εkt​; the derivative should be read as that of expected damages. And ΔDi\Delta D_iΔDi​ is a function of the whole excess-load path, so it changes as subsidies change installations elsewhere. This is the government's objective: the sum of household surplus from the solar decision minus the present value of environmental damages from dispatchable generation.

The first term integrates ViV_iVi​ from equation (3) over all households in all states. Because utility is quasi-linear, ViV_iVi​ is in dollars and can be added across households with equal weights; there is no redistributive motive. The parts of utility that were dropped in deriving (3), yi−pjei⋆+νiy_i-p_je_i^\star+\nu_iyi​−pj​ei⋆​+νi​, do not depend on subsidies and are omitted. In the quantitative model the integral includes the logit shock, so each household contributes its expected surplus,

Eϵ[Vi]=σlog⁡(1+exp⁡(vi/σ)),\mathbb{E}_\epsilon\left[V_i\right]=\sigma\log\left(1+\exp\left(v_i/\sigma\right)\right),Eϵ​[Vi​]=σlog(1+exp(vi​/σ)),

with viv_ivi​ the deterministic value of installing from equation (7). Note that ViV_iVi​ includes the subsidies received: a dollar of subsidy to an installer is a dollar of welfare here, and its cost appears only through the budget constraint (15).

The second term, D(ELoad)D(ELoad)D(ELoad), is the externality: local pollutants valued with AP3 and greenhouse gases valued at the social cost of carbon, generated by the plants that serve excess load. Households ignore it when they choose, which is the reason for subsidies. It depends on subsidies in every state through residential solar production and equation (9).

What is not in the objective: producer surplus of installers and generators (installation and retail prices are fixed), the cost-shifting implied by net metering, and the welfare of taxpayers other than through the multiplier λ\lambdaλ introduced in (16). The government chooses the three subsidies sjkWh,sjPanel,sjCosts_j^{kWh},s_j^{Panel},s_j^{Cost}sjkWh​,sjPanel​,sjCost​ in every state to maximize this subject to (15).

This is the government's budget constraint. The left-hand side is the present value of total subsidy payments: for each state jjj, integrate over its households IjI_jIj​ the subsidy sijs_{ij}sij​ paid to household iii if it installs, times the installation indicator mi⋆m_i^\starmi⋆​. The per-installer subsidy is

sij=sjPanelNi⋆+sjkWhAiNi⋆+sjCostpjIns(Ni⋆),s_{ij}=s_j^{Panel}N_i^\star+s_j^{kWh}A_iN_i^\star+s_j^{Cost}p_j^{Ins}(N_i^\star),sij​=sjPanel​Ni⋆​+sjkWh​Ai​Ni⋆​+sjCost​pjIns​(Ni⋆​),

so spending depends on subsidies directly (the rates), through who installs (mi⋆m_i^\starmi⋆​), and through system size (Ni⋆N_i^\starNi⋆​). The right-hand side GGG is an exogenous budget, set in the main counterfactual to the present value of what the current federal and state subsidies cost in the model. The exercise is therefore budget neutral: it asks how the same money should be reallocated across states and instruments.

A single national constraint means money is fungible across states; who actually pays (federal or state taxpayers) is not modeled. The constraint is what makes the problem nontrivial in a second-best sense: payments go to all installers, including those who would have installed anyway, so the cost of inducing one additional installation is larger than the subsidy that household receives. With a fixed GGG, the multiplier λ\lambdaλ in the Lagrangian (16) is endogenous and measures the welfare value of one more dollar of budget. Since a dollar paid to installers raises ∫Vidi\int V_idi∫Vi​di by a dollar and the objective (14) attaches no cost to spending, a government without a budget would spend without limit; the constraint therefore binds and λ>0\lambda>0λ>0. The alternative used in the paper is to drop the constraint and fix λ\lambdaλ as an exogenous marginal cost of public funds (equation (19)).

The government maximizes (14) over the subsidy rates {sjkWh,sjPanel,sjCost}j\{s_j^{kWh},s_j^{Panel},s_j^{Cost}\}_j{sjkWh​,sjPanel​,sjCost​}j​ subject to the inequality constraint (15). Write the constraint as h(s)≤0h(s)\le 0h(s)≤0 with

h(s)≡∑j∫i∈Ijsijmi⋆di−G.h(s)\equiv\sum_j\int_{i\in I_j}s_{ij}m_i^\star di-G.h(s)≡j∑​∫i∈Ij​​sij​mi⋆​di−G.

Attach a multiplier λ≥0\lambda\ge 0λ≥0 to it and subtract λh(s)\lambda h(s)λh(s) from the objective:

W=∫iVidi−D(ELoad)−λ(∑j∫i∈Ijsijmi⋆di−G).W=\int_iV_idi-D(ELoad)-\lambda\left(\sum_j\int_{i\in I_j}s_{ij}m_i^\star di-G\right).W=∫i​Vi​di−D(ELoad)−λ(j∑​∫i∈Ij​​sij​mi⋆​di−G).

The Kuhn-Tucker conditions for an optimum are stationarity, feasibility and complementary slackness:

∂W∂sjθ=0  for all j,θ,h(s)≤0,λ≥0,λh(s)=0.\frac{\partial W}{\partial s_j^\theta}=0\ \text{ for all }j,\theta,\qquad h(s)\le 0,\qquad \lambda\ge 0,\qquad \lambda h(s)=0.∂sjθ​∂W​=0  for all j,θ,h(s)≤0,λ≥0,λh(s)=0.

Stationarity is worked out in equation (17). The multiplier has the usual envelope interpretation: if W⋆(G)W^\star(G)W⋆(G) is the maximized value of (14) given the budget, then

dW⋆(G)dG=λ,\frac{dW^\star(G)}{dG}=\lambda,dGdW⋆(G)​=λ,

so λ\lambdaλ is the welfare gain, in dollars, from one more dollar of subsidy budget. This is why it is read as the marginal cost of public funds: each dollar of subsidy spending is charged at λ\lambdaλ rather than at one. In the budget-neutral exercise λ\lambdaλ is solved for jointly with the subsidies so that spending equals GGG; in the unconstrained exercise (19) it is instead fixed at an outside value and GGG drops out.

In the logit model the indicator mi→θ\overrightarrow{m_i}^{\theta}mi​​θ is the density of switchers implied by equation (8), and mi⋆m_i^\starmi⋆​ is replaced by πi\pi_iπi​:

mi→θ=∂πi∂sjθ=1σπi(1−πi)∂sij∂sjθ.\overrightarrow{m_i}^{\theta}=\frac{\partial\pi_i}{\partial s_j^\theta}=\frac{1}{\sigma}\pi_i(1-\pi_i)\frac{\partial s_{ij}}{\partial s_j^\theta}.mi​​θ=∂sjθ​∂πi​​=σ1​πi​(1−πi​)∂sjθ​∂sij​​.

The private surplus of additional households is absent because they are indifferent at the margin; the transfer to nonadditional households is worth one dollar to them and costs λ\lambdaλ, hence the factor 1−λ1-\lambda1−λ. All damage terms are evaluated at the excess load under the optimal subsidies, which is why the condition has to be solved numerically.

This is the main auxiliary regression for the indirect-inference estimation of household parameters, run on census tracts within 10 miles of a state border. The dependent variable is the log number of installations in tract ℓ\ellℓ; μℓ\mu_\ellμℓ​ is the average monetary benefit (thousands of dollars) of a standardized 15-panel system in the tract, computed from equation (4); ZℓZ_\ellZℓ​ contains tract demographics (college share, Democratic vote share) and state income, sales and property tax rates; ωborder(ℓ)\omega_{border(\ell)}ωborder(ℓ)​ is a fixed effect for each pair of adjacent states; εℓ\varepsilon_\ellεℓ​ is the error.

With border-pair fixed effects, α\alphaα is identified from differences between tracts on opposite sides of the same state border. Such tracts have similar sunlight and similar households but face different state subsidies and retail prices, hence different μℓ\mu_\ellμℓ​. The identifying assumption is that unobserved tastes for solar are continuous at the border; the paper supports it by showing no jump in education, partisanship or income.

The regression is not the structural model, but it has a close model counterpart. If tract ℓ\ellℓ has HℓH_\ellHℓ​ households with similar installation probability πℓ\pi_\ellπℓ​, then Mℓ≈HℓπℓM_\ell\approx H_\ell\pi_\ellMℓ​≈Hℓ​πℓ​ and equation (8) gives

∂log⁡Mℓ∂μℓ≈∂log⁡πℓ∂μℓ=1σ(1−πℓ)≈1σ.\frac{\partial\log M_\ell}{\partial\mu_\ell}\approx\frac{\partial\log\pi_\ell}{\partial\mu_\ell}=\frac{1}{\sigma}\left(1-\pi_\ell\right)\approx\frac{1}{\sigma}.∂μℓ​∂logMℓ​​≈∂μℓ​∂logπℓ​​=σ1​(1−πℓ​)≈σ1​.

So α\alphaα is essentially an estimate of 1/σ1/\sigma1/σ; the data give α\alphaα of about 0.080.080.08, and the structural estimate σ^=11.6\hat{\sigma}=11.6σ^=11.6 implies 1/σ^≈0.0861/\hat{\sigma}\approx 0.0861/σ^≈0.086. Indirect inference does not impose this approximation: it simulates tracts from the model, runs the same regression on simulated data, and chooses parameters so that the simulated α\alphaα, together with tract-level log installation rates and average panels per system, match the data. Using a fixed 15-panel system in μℓ\mu_\ellμℓ​ keeps the regressor from depending on the endogenous system size.

This is the objective for the unconstrained counterfactual. Compared with the Lagrangian (16), the budget GGG is dropped and λ\lambdaλ is no longer a multiplier to be solved for: it is an exogenous marginal cost of public funds, the welfare cost of raising one dollar of revenue elsewhere in the tax system. The paper uses λ=1\lambda=1λ=1 as the baseline and 1.251.251.25 and 1.51.51.5 as alternatives. The question changes from how to allocate a fixed budget to how much should be spent in total.

The first-order conditions are exactly equation (17), because GGG is a constant in (16) and drops out when differentiating; only the value of λ\lambdaλ differs. With λ=1\lambda=1λ=1 subsidies are pure transfers, the mechanical term vanishes, and (17) reduces to

∂Mj∂sjθ(ΔDj→θ,ext−sj→θ,ext)+∂Nj∂sjθ∣Ma(ΔDj→θ,int−∂s∂Nj→θ,int)=0.\frac{\partial M_j}{\partial s_j^\theta}\left(\overrightarrow{\Delta D_j}^{\theta,ext}-\overrightarrow{s_j}^{\theta,ext}\right)+\frac{\partial N_j}{\partial s_j^\theta}\Big|_{M^a}\left(\overrightarrow{\Delta D_j}^{\theta,int}-\overrightarrow{\frac{\partial s}{\partial N_j}}^{\theta,int}\right)=0.∂sjθ​∂Mj​​(ΔDj​​θ,ext−sj​​θ,ext)+∂sjθ​∂Nj​​​Ma​​ΔDj​​θ,int−∂Nj​∂s​​θ,int​=0.

This is a Pigouvian condition: on each margin the average subsidy paid to marginal units equals the average damages they offset. If subsidies could be tailored to each household, the solution would be a per-panel subsidy equal to ΔDi\Delta D_iΔDi​ from equation (13); with state-level instruments it holds on average across the marginal households of each state. With λ>1\lambda>1λ>1, the term (1−λ)Mj∂sij/∂sjθ‾(1-\lambda)M_j\overline{\partial s_{ij}/\partial s_j^\theta}(1−λ)Mj​∂sij​/∂sjθ​​ is negative: every dollar paid to households who would install anyway now has a net cost of λ−1\lambda-1λ−1, so optimal subsidies fall below the Pigouvian level, and by more where there are many nonadditional installers.

Quantitatively, with λ=1\lambda=1λ=1 optimal spending is 57 percent of current spending, and it falls sharply as λ\lambdaλ rises, so current national funding is above what the offset damages justify.

This extension modifies the latent dispatch function (11) to allow for transmission congestion. Here RRR is plant kkk's own NERC region and ELoad‾R\overline{ELoad}_RELoadR​ is a threshold, the 75th percentile of that region's excess load.

When own-region excess load is below the threshold (first branch), the plant behaves as in the baseline: it responds to a quadratic in the excess load of every region R′R'R′ in its interconnection Rk\mathbf{R}_kRk​, so power can flow freely across regions. When own-region excess load is above the threshold (second branch), lines into and out of the region are assumed to be congested, and the plant responds only to its own region's excess load, with a separate set of coefficients ψk0,Cons,ψk1,Cons,ψk2,Cons\psi_k^{0,Cons},\psi_k^{1,Cons},\psi_k^{2,Cons}ψk0,Cons​,ψk1,Cons​,ψk2,Cons​. The shock εkt\varepsilon_{kt}εkt​ and the censoring at zero and at capacity in equation (10) are unchanged, so the model is still a plant-level Tobit, now with regime-specific coefficients, estimated by maximum likelihood on the two subsamples of hours.

The economic content is in the cross-region derivatives. In the congested regime,

∂fk∂ELoadR′t=0  for R′≠R,∂fk∂ELoadRt=ψk1,Cons+2ψk2,ConsELoadRt.\frac{\partial f_k}{\partial ELoad_{R't}}=0\ \text{ for }R'\ne R,\qquad \frac{\partial f_k}{\partial ELoad_{Rt}}=\psi_k^{1,Cons}+2\psi_k^{2,Cons}ELoad_{Rt}.∂ELoadR′t​∂fk​​=0  for R′=R,∂ELoadRt​∂fk​​=ψk1,Cons​+2ψk2,Cons​ELoadRt​.

Rooftop solar in a region then displaces only local plants in high-load hours, and solar in other regions displaces nothing in RRR. This changes ∂Dt/∂ERtSolar\partial D_t/\partial E_{Rt}^{Solar}∂Dt​/∂ERtSolar​ in equation (13): a clean region can no longer export its solar to displace dirty generation elsewhere at peak, and a dirty region's solar is fully credited with local reductions. The specification is a simple regime switch: the threshold is imposed rather than estimated, and the latent function need not be continuous at the threshold. With it, current spending exceeds the unconstrained optimum by about 45 percent rather than over 70 percent.
